name: Meissen baroque porcelain
summary: The first true European hard-paste porcelain. The factory at Meissen paints it with a bright enamel palette, models it in full baroque relief, and gilds the edge, for the court of Saxony.

philosophy.core_thesis: Once Europe can make porcelain, it shows the fact: a white body that is modelled in a sculptural mass and painted in every enamel colour.
design_principles: Fire the hard paste at 1400 °C in reduction so that it turns dense and translucent.
Paint with a palette of 10 or more overglaze enamel colours, and fire them at 800 °C.
Model the form in relief: swans, shells, reeds, and applied flowers, as in a sculpture.
Divide a plate into a moulded rim and a painted well; add gold on the edge.
Paint harbour scenes, Chinese figures and flowers in panels called reserves, framed by gold scroll work.
Mark the base with the crossed swords, painted in cobalt under the glaze.
Make the whole service for one patron, with his arms or his initials on each piece.
anti_patterns: A buff earthenware body with a thick tin glaze
A printed pattern with a single colour
A thin, pale rococo form with pastel grounds

form.shape: Tureens, plates with a moulded rim, sauceboats, covered bowls, and large dishes, with modelled handles and knops.
form.profile: A full, curved body with a moulded border; the rim carries relief of shells, scrolls or basket weave in a regular pattern.
form.foot_and_rim: A low ring foot with a glazed base and the crossed swords; the rim is moulded, with a gilt edge.
form.proportion: Plate diameter 22 to 26 cm and wall 3 to 5 mm thick; a tureen may be 35 cm long.
rules: Mould the border in relief and keep the well flat for the painting.
Model each knop and handle as a figure: a swan, a fruit or a flower.
Gild the edge of each rim and each handle.

bodies.rule: Use a hard paste of kaolin, feldspar and quartz, which fires dense and white. Do not use earthenware, and do not use bone china: it did not exist.

methods: slip casting of figures and handles
modelling by hand for the master models
luting of cast and applied parts
gilding with gold in a binder
forming.joins: Cast handles, knops and flowers are luted with slip on the leather-hard body; silver mounts are fixed after the firing.
forming.details: A fine slip seam on a cast part, a crossed-swords mark in blue under the glaze, and a number cut in the base.

glaze.pattern: Chinoiserie scenes, harbour views, flowers and birds in reserves, with gold scroll work and applied flowers.
glaze.gloss: Bright gloss, about 80 to 95 GU, on a very white ground.
glaze.wear: The gold wears at the rim and handles; the enamel colours stay fresh on the hard glaze.

palette.strategy: A pure white ground with the full enamel palette: strong red, yellow and green, a purple, a turquoise, and gold.

firing.kiln: A wood-fired kiln, with saggars, with a first firing for the biscuit and a second for the glaze; the enamel goes in a small muffle kiln.
processes: glaze firing at about 1400 °C in reduction
gold firing at a lower heat
firing.scale: A manufactory of hundreds of painters, modellers and gilders under a royal director.
firing.signs: The crossed swords in blue under the glaze, an incised model number, and a fine slip seam on cast parts.

pieces.form: Large lidded tureen modelled with swans and reeds, painted with scenes
Plate with a moulded basket-weave rim and a coat of arms in the well
Shell-shaped boat with a modelled handle and applied flowers
Oval dish with a gilt edge and harbour scenes in reserves
Plate with a blue onion pattern painted under the glaze

positive: enamel palette harbour scene in reserve

canonical_works.maker: Johann Joachim Kändler and Johann Friedrich Eberlein, Meissen

emotion.target_response: A proud, festive abundance: the viewer sees a table that a prince has set, with white, gold and colour on every piece.

use_cases: a museum label on early European porcelain
avoid_when: the brief wants a quiet minimal form
the brief needs a pale rococo ground
the brief wants an industrial or printed pattern

modifiers.how: Change to a soft-paste body with a pastel ground colour and reserves, and thin the relief.
Change to a cream earthenware with a clear lead glaze, drop the modelling, and keep a plain rim.
Keep the porcelain, drop the enamel and the gold, and paint in cobalt in panels.
